overview.title: BatchGenerator and the single training step (listing 2.9)
overview.chapter: 2 The mathematical building blocks of neural networks
overview.section: 2.5 Looking back at our first example
overview.main_topic: Completing the BatchGenerator, the four tasks of a training step, listing 2.9 one_training_step (forward pass, sparse categorical crossentropy, gradients, weight update), and the start of the weight-update explanation
overview.central_idea: A training step on one batch is four operations: predict, compute the loss against the true labels, compute the gradient of the loss with respect to the model's weights, and move the weights a small amount against the gradient. Listing 2.9 writes this as a six-line function, leaving the gradient computation and the update as two functions still to be defined.
overview.importance: This is the heart of training, the code equivalent of steps 1-5 of mini-batch SGD on p.68 and of what fit did 2,345 times on p.76. Every custom training loop in the book (chapter 7, p.239) has this same structure.
learning_objectives: Explain how BatchGenerator slices consecutive batches and why num_batches uses math.ceil.
List the four tasks of a training step and map each to a line of listing 2.9.
Explain what ops.sparse_categorical_crossentropy returns and why it is averaged.
Describe the role of the two not-yet-defined functions get_gradients_of_loss_wrt_weights and update_weights.
State the purpose of the weight-update step: move the weights a bit in a direction that reduces the loss on this batch.

paragraphs.excerpt: The most difficult part of the process is the “training step”: updating
paragraphs.what_it_says: The training step, updating the model's weights after running it on one batch, is the most difficult part. It requires computing predictions for the batch, computing the loss given the true labels, computing the gradient of the loss with respect to the weights, and moving the weights a small amount opposite to the gradient (the four bullets).
paragraphs.what_it_means: The four bullets are the per-batch body of mini-batch SGD from p.68 (whose step 1, drawing a batch, is now handled by BatchGenerator). The first two bullets are the forward pass and only need tensor operations already explained in section 2.3. The third is the backward pass, which is why the step is 'difficult': it needs derivatives of the whole chain of operations. The fourth is the update, whose direction is minus the gradient because the gradient points toward increasing loss.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Everything else in training (batching, looping over epochs, logging) is bookkeeping around this step. Recognizing the four parts lets you read any training code, in any framework.
paragraphs.technical_idea: In symbols: \hat y = f(x; w); L = loss(y, \hat y); g = \nabla_w L; w \leftarrow w - \eta g.

terminology.meaning: One weight update computed from one batch of data.
The model's outputs for the batch, here (128, 10) class probabilities.
The direction of steepest local decrease of the loss.

connections: p.68: the five-step mini-batch SGD algorithm.
p.64: the training loop's step 4 identified as the difficult part.
p.239: the same three/four-step structure for custom loops in chapter 7.

paragraphs.excerpt: As you already know, the purpose of the “weight update” step (represented
paragraphs.what_it_says: The weight-update step, represented by update_weights(), moves the weights by 'a bit' in a direction that reduces the loss on this batch; the magnitude of the move is determined by the learning rate (the sentence ends on p.80).
paragraphs.what_it_means: The update needs a direction (minus the gradient) and a step size (the learning rate, a small scalar). Too large a step can overshoot the minimum; too small a step makes training slow. Only the loss on the current batch is considered, which is the stochastic aspect of SGD.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It introduces the implementation on p.80, w.assign(w - g * learning_rate), and the Keras optimizer that replaces it.

terminology.meaning: Scalar factor that sets how far the weights move along the negative gradient in one step.

connections: p.80: update_weights implemented by hand and with optimizers.SGD.

concepts.name: Mini-batch iteration (BatchGenerator)
concepts.definition: Handing out consecutive slices of batch_size images and labels, keeping track of the current position with an index.
concepts.intuition: A cursor moving through the dataset 128 rows at a time.
concepts.technical: num_batches = ceil(N / batch_size); next() returns data[index:index+batch_size] and advances index.
concepts.significance: Supplies the batches that one_training_step consumes; replaces fit's built-in batching.
concepts.example: N = 60000, batch_size = 128: num_batches = ceil(468.75) = 469; the last batch has 96 samples.
concepts.misconception: BatchGenerator does not shuffle the data; it serves batches in the stored order.

concepts.name: Training step
concepts.definition: Running the model on one batch, computing the loss, computing the gradient of the loss with regard to the weights, and moving the weights a small amount opposite to the gradient.
concepts.intuition: Try, measure the error, find which way each knob should turn, turn the knobs a little.
concepts.technical: Listing 2.9: forward pass -> sparse categorical crossentropy -> gradients wrt model.weights -> update_weights.
concepts.significance: The atomic unit of learning; fit on p.76 performs 2,345 of them.
concepts.example: One call of one_training_step on a (128, 784) batch updates all four weight tensors once.
concepts.misconception: A training step does not process the whole dataset; it uses one batch.

concepts.name: Sparse categorical crossentropy
concepts.definition: Loss comparing predicted class probabilities to integer labels; ops.sparse_categorical_crossentropy returns one value per sample.
concepts.intuition: Penalizes the model by how little probability it gave to the correct digit.
concepts.technical: For sample i: L_i = -log p_{i, y_i}. ops.mean averages these over the batch.
concepts.significance: The loss chosen in compile on p.76, now called explicitly.
concepts.misconception: The function does not return a single number for the batch; it returns a vector of per-sample losses (hence the ops.mean).

concepts.name: Gradient descent update
concepts.definition: Moving the weights a small amount in the direction opposite to the gradient of the loss, with the step size set by the learning rate.
concepts.intuition: Take a small step downhill on the loss surface.
concepts.technical: w <- w - learning_rate * dL/dw, applied to every tensor in model.weights.
concepts.significance: The fourth bullet and the update_weights function.
concepts.misconception: The update does not jump to the minimum; it moves 'a bit', and many steps are needed.

code.title: BatchGenerator (rest of the class)
code.original_code:
assert len(images) == len(labels)
        self.index = 0
        self.images = images
        self.labels = labels
        self.batch_size = batch_size
        self.num_batches = math.ceil(len(images) / batch_size)

    def next(self):
        images = self.images[self.index : self.index + self.batch_size]
        labels = self.labels[self.index : self.index + self.batch_size]
        self.index += self.batch_size
        return images, labels

code.title: A single step of training
code.original_code:
def one_training_step(model, images_batch, labels_batch):
    predictions = model(images_batch)
    loss = ops.sparse_categorical_crossentropy(labels_batch, predictions)
    average_loss = ops.mean(loss)
    gradients = get_gradients_of_loss_wrt_weights(loss, model.weights)
    update_weights(gradients, model.weights)
    return loss
code.what_it_does: Performs one training step on a batch: forward pass, loss computation, gradient computation with respect to all model weights, and weight update.

pitfalls: As printed, average_loss is computed but `loss` (the per-sample vector) is what is passed to the gradient function and returned. A gradient of a vector target is usually taken as the gradient of its sum, which is batch_size times the gradient of the mean, effectively scaling the learning rate. The rewritten version on p.81 fixes this: it calls tape.gradient(average_loss, model.weights) and returns average_loss.
The function cannot run yet: get_gradients_of_loss_wrt_weights and update_weights are defined on p.80.
The gradient computation must 'see' the forward pass; with TensorFlow this means running lines 2-4 inside a GradientTape (p.80).

deeper.title: Mapping listing 2.9 to the SGD algorithm of p.68
deeper.body:
| p.68 step | Listing 2.9 / this page |
|---|---|
| 1. Draw a batch x, y_true | `BatchGenerator.next()` |
| 2. Forward pass y_pred = model(x) | `predictions = model(images_batch)` |
| 3. Loss of y_pred vs y_true | `ops.sparse_categorical_crossentropy(...)`, `ops.mean(loss)` |
| 4. Backward pass: gradient | `get_gradients_of_loss_wrt_weights(loss, model.weights)` |
| 5. Move parameters opposite to the gradient | `update_weights(gradients, model.weights)` |

deeper.title: Why 'difficult'? The gradient is the only non-obvious part
deeper.body:
1. Predictions and loss are just compositions of matmul, add, relu, softmax, log and mean, all explained in section 2.3.
2. The update is one subtraction per tensor.
3. The gradient requires the derivative of the loss with respect to 407,050 scalars through softmax and two Dense layers. Writing these derivatives by hand is error-prone, which is why p.80 hands this job to automatic differentiation (`tf.GradientTape`), as the chain rule of p.70-p.74 is applied mechanically by the framework.

questions.question: Which of the four tasks of a training step is the 'backward pass'?
options: Compute the predictions for the images in the batch
Compute the loss value given the actual labels
Compute the gradient of the loss with regard to the model's weights
Move the weights a small amount opposite to the gradient
questions.answer: Compute the gradient of the loss with regard to the model's weights
questions.explanation: p.68 calls computing the gradient the backward pass. Predictions are the forward pass, the loss is computed from the forward outputs, and moving the weights is the update.

questions.question: For a dataset of 1,000 samples and batch_size=128, what is num_batches and how many samples are in the last batch?
questions.explanation: ceil(1000/128) = ceil(7.8125) = 8. Seven full batches cover 896 samples, leaving 104.

questions.question: What does get_gradients_of_loss_wrt_weights return, according to the callout?
questions.answer: A list of gradients in which each entry corresponds to a weight in the model.weights list.
questions.explanation: The callout states this explicitly; the list therefore has 4 entries with the shapes of W1, b1, W2, b2.

questions.question: What does the page say determines the magnitude of the weight update?
questions.explanation: The weight update paragraph says the magnitude of the move is determined by the learning rate (completed on p.80). The gradient also scales the step, but batch size and epochs do not set the step magnitude directly.

questions.question: A batch of two samples has true-class predicted probabilities 0.5 and 0.25. Compute loss and average_loss from listing 2.9 (natural log).
Listing 2.9 computes average_loss but passes loss to the gradient function. What difference could this make, and what would you pass instead?
questions.answer: If the framework treats a vector target as its sum, the gradient is batch_size times the gradient of the mean, which acts like a larger learning rate. Passing average_loss (a scalar) makes the update independent of batch size.
questions.explanation: This observation goes beyond the book's text; the printed listing is reproduced verbatim. Gradients are defined for scalar losses (p.80: 'gradient of any scalar value'). The rewritten step on p.81 indeed uses tape.gradient(average_loss, model.weights).
